How much longer must it be?
Shmuel first considers twice as long.
Rav says any extra length suffices.
The discussion returns to the disciple’s statement in the mishna.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva says the school dispute covers both narrow and wide alleyways.
How does this differ from the first tanna?
They differ over the rule for an alleyway under four handbreadths, though attribution is uncertain.
A baraita says Rabbi Yishmael did not state the student’s view yet calls it law.
Those two clauses appear inconsistent.
Shmuel says Rabbi Akiva praised the student to sharpen his peers, without ruling that way.
Another reading says the student’s view merely appeared reasonable.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi identifies the student as Rabbi Meir.
One account has Rabbi Meir study with Rabbi Yishmael and then Rabbi Akiva.
A conflicting account reverses the order and records Rabbi Yishmael’s warning to scribes.
Rabbi Meir describes iron sulfate ink, and Rabbi Yishmael objects that sota text must erase.
How does the ink answer a warning about omitted or extra letters?
Rabbi Meir says the ink also guards against a fly altering a letter.
The accounts still differ about teacher order and who forbade the ink.
Rabbi Meir may have moved from Rabbi Akiva to Rabbi Yishmael and back.
The conflicting attributions of the prohibition remain unresolved.
Two reports differ on how broadly iron sulfate is barred in writing sota passages.
What practical difference separates them?
It concerns erasing a sota passage from a Torah scroll.
A separate dispute concerns reusing one woman’s sota scroll for another.
Rav Pappa distinguishes a named scroll from a Torah scroll written without a specific woman.
Rav Nahman distinguishes a scroll written for some sota from a Torah scroll written for study.
A mishna about a bill of divorce begins a further challenge.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A divorce document written for one couple cannot serve another identically named couple.
Divorce requires writing for her; the sota ritual requires performance for her, namely erasure.
Rabbi Aha praises Rabbi Meir’s unmatched ability to argue both sides of a law.
A baraita explains the names Meir and Nehorai as illumination in legal learning.
Rabbi says seeing Rabbi Meir as his teacher sharpened his learning.
Sumakhus is said to give forty-eight reasons on either side of purity questions.
A Yavne student could offer many arguments for purifying a creeping creature.
Ravina proposes an inference from a snake’s purity.
A snake merely acts like a thorn; the inference fails.
A heavenly voice recognizes both schools’ words yet rules for Beit Hillel.
Why was Beit Hillel’s opinion selected if both are valid teachings?
They were patient and presented Beit Shammai’s teaching before their own.
Their debate about a sukka table illustrates that manner of presenting the other view.
The passage draws lessons about humility, status, and patience.
The schools debate whether creation was better for humankind and conclude with self-examination.
The new mishna specifies a beam wide enough to hold a small brick.
It discusses beam strength and Rabbi Yehuda’s leniency for weak material.
It treats curved and round beams by imagined straightening or squaring.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does the mishna allow a one-handbreadth beam when a small brick is a handbreadth and a half wide?
A handbreadth supports the brick once plaster secures the extra half handbreadth at its sides.
Rabba bar Rav Huna requires the beam, but not its supports, to bear the brick.
Rav Hisda requires both the beam and its supports to bear the beam and brick.
Rav Sheshet describes a mat hung from a beam but ending three handbreadths above ground.
It is neither a visible beam nor a valid partition, since the beam is hidden and goats can pass underneath.
A baraita joins beams across gaps under three handbreadths but requires another beam at three.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel extends that joining rule to gaps under four handbreadths.
Two narrow beams together suffice when they can support a brick along its handbreadth width.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel instead tests whether they can support its three-handbreadth length.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda treats stacked beams as joined within the permitted height limits.
Abaye explains that the son agrees with his father about treating separated beams as joined.
He differs from his father by retaining the twenty-cubit upper limit.
Rav corrects the teaching of Rabbi Yehuda’s mishna: the beam must be both wide and sturdy.
Rav elsewhere permits a four-handbreadth beam even when it cannot bear a brick.
A beam four handbreadths wide is treated differently, as a roof edge.
Why repeat the imagined-strength rule for a straw beam?
The rule applies even when no beam of that material could bear a brick.
The mishna treats a curved beam as though it were straight.
Why is this rule needed?
Rabbi Zeira applies it when the bend leaves the alley or permitted heights, provided the remaining gap is under three handbreadths.
Why is Rabbi Zeira’s qualification not already evident?
An outward bend could seem to draw a person beyond the alley; the rule dismisses that concern.
The mishna treats a round beam as though it were square.
Why repeat another imagined-shape rule?
The clause teaches the circumference-to-diameter measure of three to one.
What is the source of that measure?
The verse gives Solomon’s round sea a ten-cubit diameter and a thirty-cubit circumference.
The sea’s brim seems to add thickness to one measurement.
Its lily-shaped brim is exceptionally thin, as the second verse describes.
Even a thin brim has some thickness.
The circumference is measured from the inside as well.
Rabbi Hiyya says Solomon’s sea held the volume of 150 ritual baths.
How much water does one ritual bath require?
The baraita begins deriving the forty-seah measure from the verse about washing the whole body.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The bathing verse requires immersion of the whole body in a three-cubic-cubit bath containing forty seah.
A five-hundred-cubic-cubit sea seems more than sufficient for 150 baths of three cubic cubits each.
That calculation assumes a square vessel, whereas Solomon’s sea was round.
After subtracting a quarter for roundness, the sea appears to hold only 125 baths.
Its lower three cubits were square and only its upper two cubits were round.
Why not make just the top cubit round?
The stated two thousand bat, at three seah per bat, supports the proposed volume.
Chronicles instead says that the sea held three thousand bat.
That larger amount refers to a heaped dry measure.
Abaye infers that a dry measure heaped above the rim adds one third.
A mishna compares vessels holding forty seah of liquid with two kor of dry goods.
The mishna requires a ten-handbreadth side post of any width, while Rabbi Yosei requires three handbreadths.
Does the mishna’s plural side posts support Rabbi Eliezer’s requirement of two?
The plural may simply refer to side posts in general.
If so, why does the preceding mishna use the singular for a cross beam?
The mishna invokes the posts disputed by Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages without deciding how many are required.
How thin may a side post of any width be?
Rabbi Hiyya allows even a garment tie’s thickness.
A baraita limits carrying to the inner half when the post stands halfway down the alley.
Why is that necessary to state?
It permits the inner half despite the missing post at the entrance.
Why is even that permission necessary?
One might fear use of the entire alley; the baraita permits the inner half.
Rava invalidates a post separated three handbreadths from the ground or wall.
Even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s joining rule does not heal a ground gap that goats can pass through.
Shmuel’s ruling as reported by Rav Yosef rejects Rabbi Yosei on both brine and side posts.
Rav Huna bar Hinana recalls hearing the ruling for brine but not for side posts.
Why distinguish side posts from brine when the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yosei in both?
Rabbi’s view supports Rabbi Yosei on side posts.
Rav Rahumei reports another chain transmitting rejection of Rabbi Yosei on both questions.
The speaker later denies having said that ruling.
Rava insists he learned it directly, then explains the speaker retracted because Rabbi Yosei’s reasons carry weight.
Rava bar Rav Hanan asks Abaye for the accepted side-post ruling.
Abaye points to common practice using minimal-width posts.
Another version places the question after a dispute about the blessing before drinking water.
Rav Hanan asks Abaye which blessing is the law.
Abaye again directs him to observe common practice.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye accepts a side post that arose without design; Rava rejects it.
Both reject such a post if residents did not rely on it before Shabbat.
When they did rely on it, Abaye accepts it and Rava still requires deliberate construction.
Does their dispute also extend to an unintended partition?
Trees may serve as walls of a valid sukka.
They may have been planted for that purpose; the rule still dispels a concern about using the tree.
A tree, fence, or reed screen can form a well-side partition.
Those too may be deliberate; the novelty is that closely spaced reeds join.
Branches close to the ground allow carrying beneath a tree.
The tree may have been planted to enclose that space.
If so, why does another ruling limit the enclosed area to two beit seah?
A space used to serve the surrounding field remains subject to that size limit.
A Shabbat abode on a mound, in a hollow, or among standing grain gains its enclosed area and the ordinary outer limit.
Deliberate construction cannot explain natural mounds and hollows.
All accept natural partitions; the side-post dispute turns on whether a post is a partition or a visible marker.
Protruding stones form a post when gaps between them are under three handbreadths.
The stones may have been placed deliberately; the rule dispels the impression that they only join buildings.
A recessed part of a wall can count as a post when visible from either side.
It may have been shaped deliberately; the teaching establishes that outside visibility suffices.
After an alley post falls, Rav declines to rely on a nearby palm because it had not been relied on before Shabbat.
His reason implies that prior reliance would make the palm a valid post.
Could Abaye and Rava then dispute only the case without prior reliance?
Their longstanding dispute over a balcony support shows that prior reliance does not settle their disagreement.
The mishna allows an animal as a side post, while Rabbi Meir forbids it.
The mishna begins the parallel rule for using an animal as a grave cover.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna completes the grave-cover dispute and contrasts the rulings on writing a divorce document on a living creature.
A baraita lists Rabbi Meir’s objections to living partitions and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili’s objection to living divorce documents.
What is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili’s reason?
He reads scroll together with write for her to admit varied surfaces while excluding animate objects and food.
How do the Rabbis read scroll?
They read it as a written account rather than a restriction on the writing surface.
What then do the Rabbis derive from write for her?
Writing effects divorce; an analogy to betrothal does not allow divorce by money.
How does Rabbi Yosei HaGelili exclude divorce by money?
A scroll of severance means the document, and no other means, severs the marriage.
What do the Rabbis derive from scroll of severance?
It requires complete severance: permanent conditions fail, while a thirty-day condition can end.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives the condition rule from the expanded wording of severance.
The Rabbis do not draw that extra inference from the expanded form.
The mishna permits carrying in a caravan enclosure with ten-handbreadth walls and breaches no greater than the built part.
A breach of about ten cubits is an entrance; a wider breach invalidates the enclosure.
Rav Pappa allows equal built and breached portions; Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua forbids them.
Rav Pappa reads the rule as forbidding a majority of breach.
Rav Huna reads it as requiring a majority of standing fence.
The mishna bars breaches greater than the built part, implying equality is allowed.
The mishna could instead mean permission only when the standing part is greater.
Then it should have barred equal breaches; its wording remains difficult for Rav Huna.
A sukka is valid when proper roofing fills gaps equal to the invalid skewers.
The gaps may be slightly wider to allow insertion and removal of the skewers.
Could the gaps not have exactly equaled the skewers?
Rabbi Ami requires an added amount of valid roofing.
Rava places valid roofing across the skewers to ensure effective predominance.
A new caravan baraita is introduced as further evidence about enclosure breaches.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The caravan baraita permits carrying if gaps remain smaller than the camels or equipment between them.
Its gaps may be wide enough for easy insertion, hence wider than the standing objects.
A mixed-seeds baraita first requires gaps under three handbreadths between narrow boards.
For boards from three to four handbreadths, it restricts full-width gaps and rejects predominantly open fencing.
For wider boards it gives rules for equal gaps, facing the fence, and predominance of standing boards.
A breach over ten cubits fails unless a doorway shape spans it.
The three-to-four-handbreadth clause seems to reject Rav Pappa’s permission for equal gaps.
He can read full width as a gap slightly wider than a board, allowing insertion.
The clause forbidding a breach greater than the standing portion implies equality is allowed.
Does that refute Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua?
The latter clause permits carrying opposite a gap only when standing exceeds breach, suggesting equality fails.
The two clauses thus appear to challenge opposite sides of the dispute.
For Rav Pappa, the latter clause merely parallels the wording of the first.
For Rav Huna, the first clause likewise parallels the wording of the latter.
Rav Huna must explain why the baraita separates boards under three handbreadths from those exactly three.
The first fails when a goat can leap through; the next fails when breach equals standing fence.
Whose view joins gaps under three handbreadths?
The Rabbis apply lavud only below three handbreadths.
The next clause treats the three-to-four range separately, seeming to use a different lavud limit.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: That separate range appears to follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s four-handbreadth lavud rule.
Abaye keeps the whole baraita with the Rabbis: a four-handbreadth standing part matters even when smaller ones do not.
Rava keeps it with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: his larger lavud rule applies above ground, not through a goat-sized ground gap.
A baraita permits carrying among openings and windows only where standing wall exceeds breaches.
How could most of the walls be openings while standing wall predominates?
Read it as many openings added to walls that still have more standing material.
Equality would then be forbidden, directly contradicting Rav Pappa.
Nevertheless, the halakha is ruled according to Rav Pappa.
How can the rejected view be the practical ruling?
The mishna’s ban on breaches greater than the built part implies that equal portions are allowed.
The mishna permits a rope enclosure when three ropes leave gaps under three handbreadths.
Their combined thickness must bring the total partition to ten handbreadths.
Vertical boards also work when adjacent gaps remain under three handbreadths.
Rabbi Yehuda limits the leniency to caravans; the Rabbis call a caravan only the usual example.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda requires both horizontal and vertical elements; the Rabbis accept either.
Does standing material predominate effectively when a fence has only horizontal elements?
Abaye suggests thinner ropes and adjusted gaps should suffice if predominance can be counted horizontally.
A nearly four-handbreadth gap at ground level lets goats through.
At the top, air around the upper rope defeats that rope’s partition effect.
In the middle, the setup would prove that standing portions on two sides may combine.
The dilemma is reframed as a perforated seven-plus-handbreadth mat raised less than three handbreadths.
Rav Ashi instead frames it as a suspended partition; Rav permits that only over water.
Why does Rabbi Yehuda mention caravans if a baraita permits an individual’s partition within two beit seah?
The caravan distinction concerns enclosing all the area the group needs.
To which teaching was that explanation originally applied?
A baraita lets even an individual use ropes, contrary to Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda’s apparent demand for both directions.
The Rabbis allow needed space for individuals or caravans unless two beit seah remain unused.
The requirement for both directions concerns permission for the entire space needed.
Rav Nahman first teaches the stricter allotment of two beit seah per traveler in a caravan of three.
He is challenged for following an individual view over the Rabbis.
He retracts and rules that a caravan of three may enclose all the space it needs.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does Rav Nahman’s revised ruling combine Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda for the first cases with the Rabbis for a caravan?
Yes; Rabbi Yehuda also supports the narrower rule for individuals.
Rav Giddel transmits Rav’s surprising contrast: three may be barred in five beit seah yet allowed in seven.
Rav Ashi distinguishes a group needing six and enclosing seven from one needing five and enclosing seven.
Does the baraita’s empty two-beit-seah rule mean an area empty of people?
It means space empty of their belongings.
Rav Huna and Rabbi Yitzhak dispute whether the onset of Shabbat or the current residents determine a changed caravan’s status.
Rav Huna’s ruling on a sealed eiruv opening indicates that an initial Shabbat permission persists.
Do they simply repeat the dispute of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei?
A mishna contrasts Rabbi Yehuda’s continued permission after walls fall with Rabbi Yosei’s refusal to separate that Shabbat from later ones.
Should Rav Huna align with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yitzhak with Rabbi Yosei?
Rav Huna can also follow Rabbi Yosei, since the caravan case retains its partitions.
Rabbi Yitzhak can also follow Rabbi Yehuda, since this case loses residents rather than walls.
How do the last Rabbis differ from the mishna’s first view on rope or board partitions?
They differ over using such a partition for an individual in a settled place.
The new mishna lists four military-camp exemptions: wood, handwashing, demai, and eiruv.
A baraita extends camp rules to dry wood, encampment sites, and burial where a soldier falls.
Why permit taking dry wood when Joshua’s ordinance already permits collecting wood?
The camp rule reaches kinds of wood beyond the shrubs and thorns in Joshua’s ordinance.
Alternatively, it includes detached wood, unlike the ordinance for attached growth.
Alternatively, it includes dry wood, unlike the earlier allowance for moist wood.
Why specify burial at the place of death when an unattended corpse already acquires its place?
The military rule applies even though others are available to bury the soldier.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A camp’s burial rule applies despite available buriers; an ordinary unattended corpse acquires its place only without them.
A baraita allows moving a corpse from a public road toward the less cultivated field, challenging burial in place.
Rav Beivai limits that exception to a body obstructing a public path.
Abaye limits the camp’s handwashing exemption to washing before a meal.
Why is washing after a meal still obligatory?
Dangerous Sodomite salt can blind the eyes.
Abaye says even a tiny grain may be present among ordinary salt.
Must one wash after handling salt outside a meal?
Rav Ashi treats that obligation as obvious.
The demai exemption follows a mishna and Beit Hillel’s permission to feed demai to the poor or soldiers.
The camp eiruv exemption covers courtyard joining, not extending Shabbat travel limits.
Rabbi Hiyya teaches that overstepping the Torah’s Shabbat limit incurs lashes.
Rabbi Yonatan questions lashes for a prohibition worded with al.
Rav Aha challenges that grammatical distinction from another prohibition using al.
The deeper objection is that a warning also linked to a capital offense does not receive lashes.
Rav Ashi distinguishes the verse’s going out from carrying out, leaving travel beyond the limit as its subject.
The chapter on alleyways concludes.
The new mishna sets out Rabbi Yehuda’s four corner double posts and Rabbi Meir’s added four straight posts around wells.
It gives the posts’ minimum height and width, while allowing any thickness.
Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda differ over the width between posts and how teams of oxen are measured.
Posts may be moved closer if a cow can stand mostly inside while drinking.
The mishna begins another permitted adjustment to the well-post enclosure.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna allows expanding the well enclosure with added boards; Rabbi Yehuda limits its area to two beit seah.
The Rabbis restrict that area limit to gardens and storage enclosures, not pens, yards, or courtyards.
They permit farther expansion when additional boards are placed.
Does the mishna conflict with Hananya, who permits ropes but not posts for a cistern?
A cistern and a replenishing well may have different rules.
An alternative reading again infers that Hananya forbids posts even for wells.
Hananya replied only to the first tanna’s cistern case, without stating his full distinction.
Does the mishna conflict with Rabbi Akiva, who also allows posts around a public cistern?
The mishna names wells because its permission covers both public and private wells consistently.
Does the plural wells conflict with Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava’s restriction to public wells?
The plural may refer to wells generally without including private ones.
What does the term deyomadin mean?
Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar explains it as two posts joined at a corner.
A mnemonic introduces related teachings about the prefix deyo and Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar.
A mishna exempts inferior figs from doubtful tithes except for deyufra.
What is deyufra?
Ulla identifies a tree bearing two fruit crops yearly.
Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar describes Adam as originally having two faces and cites verses about creation.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether tzela was a face or a tail.
How does behind and before fit the view that Eve came from a tail?
Rabbi Ami reads the words as last in creation and first in punishment.
Adam was created last, but the serpent and Eve were cursed before him.
The Flood verse lists humankind first among those destroyed.
Why does the creation verb have two yods if Eve began as a tail?
The spelling evokes a person’s struggle between inclination and Creator.
How does created them male and female fit the tail view?
Rabbi Abbahu reconciles plural intent with the singular creation actually carried out.
Why mention closing flesh over the removed part if it was only a tail?
The incision itself required closure.
What needed building if Eve already existed as a face?
One interpretation takes building to mean that God braided Eve’s hair before bringing her to Adam.
Another interpretation begins describing the shape of Eve’s body as a constructed form.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The alternative interpretation compares Eve’s bodily form to a storehouse shaped to hold its contents.
God bringing Eve to Adam is read as serving as his wedding attendant, an example for a greater person.
Under the two-face account, who walked in front?
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak places the man first and cites a baraita about conduct on a path.
A baraita condemns handing money to a woman for the purpose of looking at her and cites a verse.
Rav Nahman reads Manoah walking after his wife as a sign of ignorance.
Similar wording describes Elkana and Elisha, making a literal reading implausible.
Following can mean following her advice, including in Manoah’s case.
Rav Ashi challenges Rav Nahman from a basic Torah account in which Rebecca follows the man.
Rabbi Yohanan ranks several routes to avoid appearing to follow a woman, idolatry, or a synagogue during prayer.
Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar says Adam fathered harmful spirits during years of separation, inferring it from Seth’s likeness.
Rabbi Meir’s account says Adam fasted and separated from his wife for those years.
The harmful beings are attributed to involuntary emissions.
Rabbi Yirmeya teaches that only part of a person’s praise is spoken in that person’s presence.
God calls Noah righteous when speaking to him.
Outside Noah’s presence, the verse adds that he was perfect.
The dove’s olive leaf becomes a prayer for bitter food from God rather than sweet food from people.
A matching word in Proverbs supports the reading as nourishment.
Torah heard in a house at night is associated with the house’s endurance through a verse in Job.
Since the Temple’s destruction, a two-letter divine name suffices for praise, as in the Psalm.
Rabbi Yirmeya contrasts the effects of Babylon’s and Samaria’s curses on their neighbors through prophetic verses.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse ends the prior contrast by describing Samaria as land fit for vines.
Rabbi Yirmeya contrasts a king who silences the condemned with divine judgment.
A Psalm is read as the condemned person’s silence, praise, and offering of a vow to God.
How should the Psalm about those passing through the valley of weeping be read?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads it as sinners accepting the justice of their punishment.
Reish Lakish says the wicked remain rebellious even at Gehenna’s entrance.
One teaching concerns Jewish sinners; the other concerns rebels among the nations.
Another teaching of Reish Lakish exempts Jewish sinners from Gehenna’s fire.
He argues from the gold altar’s endurance to the merits even of those described as empty.
Abraham raises those temporarily liable there, with a stated exception.
Rav Kahana questions deriving ongoing rebellion merely from a present-tense biblical form.
Rabbi Yirmeya names entrances to Gehenna in wilderness, sea, and Jerusalem.
Korah’s descent into Sheol supports the wilderness entrance.
Jonah’s prayer from Sheol supports the sea entrance.
Isaiah’s fire and furnace in Zion are read as Gehenna and its Jerusalem entrance.
A report of smoking palms in the valley of Hinnom appears to identify another entrance.
It may be the Jerusalem entrance already named.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lists seven names of Gehenna.
Verses supply six names, and a received teaching supplies the seventh.
Why is Gehenna itself absent from the list?
It is treated as a description of a valley or of futile conduct.
Why is Tofte also absent?
It is read as a description of yielding to temptation.
Reish Lakish proposes entrances to Eden in three regions, followed by praise of local fruits.
Why say the oxen are tied and also specify that they are not untied?
The wording requires actual ties, not merely the closeness of tied animals.
A Tosefta measures room for one team entering and another leaving.
A baraita gives the cow’s head-and-body length and its width for measuring the gap.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita translates the widths of six or eight oxen into approximate cubit measures.
Why call Rabbi Meir’s ten-cubit measurement approximate?
Its wording parallels the following approximate number.
Why do the later approximate thirteen and fourteen cubits both appear imprecise?
Rav Pappa fixes the width at thirteen and one-third cubits.
Rav Pappa distinguishes cistern widths: eight needs no extra posts, twelve does, and intermediate sizes divide the authorities.
What new point does Rav Pappa add to the baraita?
He reached the same measure independently without hearing it.
A mnemonic introduces Abaye’s questions to Rabba.
Can extending double posts replace separate straight posts under Rabbi Meir?
Rabba first reads increase the posts as widening existing double posts.
Abaye allows the wording to mean adding separate straight posts.
Rabba objects that the mishna should then say to increase their number.
Abaye accepts that explanatory reading of its wording.
A second version reverses the readings and favors extending the existing posts.
Above thirteen and one-third cubits, must Rabbi Yehuda add straight posts or widen corner posts?
A baraita repeats the permitted well enclosure, size limit, and distinction from ordinary courtyards.
If widened posts form full partitions, Rabbi Yehuda should have called both structures partitions.
He may distinguish full walls with ten-cubit openings from well posts with larger permitted gaps.
Can a steep mound serve as a double post?
A square stone qualifies if an imagined cut would leave the required two perpendicular arms.
A round stone qualifies if imagined squaring and cutting yield those arms.
What distinguishes the two stone rulings?
They differ on whether one may make one or two imagined alterations.
Can closely spaced reeds joined by lavud serve as a double post?
A baraita allows a tree, fence, or reed barrier to count as a double post.
The reed barrier could instead be a dense thicket.
A thicket seems redundant with the tree case.
The alternate reading is likewise redundant with fence; the baraita may list two forms of either category.
Another version asks whether a dense reed thicket qualifies.
The same baraita’s reed barrier is offered as support.
It could refer instead to reeds separated by gaps under three handbreadths.
That sounds equivalent to a fence.
The reply begins comparing this redundancy with the tree case.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The reed-baraita dispute ends without proof because either reading can yield a duplicate category.
May one carry between a courtyard opening into the well-post enclosure and the enclosure?
Rabba permits carrying between the single courtyard and enclosure.
What if two courtyards open into it?
Rabba forbids carrying in that case.
Rav Huna forbids it even after an eiruv, lest people think an eiruv alone permits the well-post space.
Rava permits the transfer when the courtyards have made an eiruv together.
Abaye cites a baraita permitting one courtyard and permitting two after a shared eiruv.
Does the baraita refute Rav Huna?
He can place its permitted case after a breach joins the two courtyards visibly.
Do the well posts still permit carrying if their water dries up on Shabbat?
Rabba says their special partition works only while water remains.
If water returns on Shabbat, is permission restored?
Abaye recalls that drying itself ended the original permission.
Returning water creates an effective Shabbat partition, as a baraita recognizes partitions arising that day.
Rav Nahman seems to recognize a newly erected Shabbat partition only to impose liability, not to permit carrying.
His restriction applies to a partition erected intentionally.
Rabbi Elazar rules that throwing into a well-post enclosure incurs liability.
Is that not obvious from the permission to draw water?
The ruling includes the same post arrangement set up without a well.
Would its validity away from a well not also be evident?
It remains a partition even where the public passes through.
Did Rabbi Elazar not already teach that public traffic leaves such partitions valid?
The mishna’s dispute about a public path and the amoraic explanation state the strength of the partitions.
The earlier explanation might report the Rabbis’ position without Rabbi Elazar endorsing it.
Why would both formulations be needed?
One formulation was inferred from the other rather than separately stated.
The mishna’s cow-space rule is compared with bringing one’s head and body into the domain where one drinks.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The same body-position rule is noted for tasting from a winepress before tithing.
Must a cow, like a person, have its head and most of its body within the drinking domain?
If one holds only the bucket, that position is required because the cow may draw it across the boundary.
Is it still required when the person holds both cow and bucket?
The well-post mishna requires the cow’s head and most of its body inside.
That mishna might involve holding only the bucket.
A baraita says not to hold filled water before the animal, seemingly banning that setup.
Abaye places the baraita at a manger crossing domains and explains a decree about repairing it while carrying a bucket.
Carrying it out after lifting it for another purpose would not create liability.
The concern is bringing the bucket back into the enclosed domain after the repair.
Another version asks whether the cow’s head and body inside suffice, as for a person.
With both bucket and cow held, this version accepts that position as sufficient.
What if only the bucket is held?
The mishna’s cow-space rule is offered as proof of sufficiency.
It might refer to holding both bucket and animal.
The baraita barring a held bucket before an animal appears to support that limit.
Abaye again locates that baraita at a manger spanning domains and explains the concern about repair.
The initial carrying out would lack the required intention at lifting.
The concern is a later return of the bucket into the private domain.
Force-feeding a camel still requires its head and most of its body inside, though the animal is held.
A camel’s long neck creates a special risk of extending into the other domain.
A second baraita says the same of an animal generally.
Animal here might also mean camel.
The baraitot use separate terms, animal and camel.
They are separate teachings; another baraita expressly singles out the camel’s long neck.
Rabbi Yitzhak bar Adda limits the well-post allowance to festival pilgrims.
Another baraita limits it to cattle.
The cattle are those belonging to festival pilgrims; the human case continues on the next daf.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior baraita concludes that a person can descend into the well to drink.
If posts serve only animals, why require potable spring water rather than collected water?
The water must also be fit for a human to drink.
The baraita allows posts for cattle and for people unable to descend, while directing water for animals into a trough.
Why then require room for the cow’s head and most of its body inside the posts?
Abaye confines the trough restriction to a special manger that spans the boundary.
Rav’s first reported version rejects watch huts in Babylonia and well posts outside the Land of Israel.
Floods threaten the huts; the well-post concession belongs to travel for religious study.
A second report excludes both huts and well posts in Babylonia and elsewhere abroad.
Floods or thieves undermine huts, while abundant water or scarce study centers undermine the post concession.
Rav Hisda asks how Marei traveled three parasangs on Shabbat if Babylonian watch huts do not count.
Marei points to closely spaced ruins of towns rather than watch huts.
Rav Hisda introduces an exposition of the Torah’s breadth through David, Job, Ezekiel, and Zechariah.
David and Job call Torah broad without giving a numerical measure.
Ezekiel describes a scroll written on both faces without its scale.
The writing is interpreted as the righteous suffering and reward and the wicked’s future punishment.
Zechariah’s measured scroll and Isaiah’s measure of the world yield a vast numerical comparison.
A second exposition begins with Jeremiah’s two baskets of figs.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Jeremiah’s verse completes the contrast between very good and very bad figs.
The baskets symbolize righteous and wicked people, both ultimately capable of yielding fragrance.
Rava reads mandrakes as young Israelites who have not tasted sin.
He reads the doors and fruits as women communicating or guarding marital intimacy.
New and old are read as Israel’s observance of later safeguards alongside Torah law.
Rav Hisda asks a scholar how to interpret new and old.
The scholar proposes light and weighty commandments.
Rav Hisda objects that the Torah was not given in separate installments.
He distinguishes Torah commandments from later rabbinic enactments.
Rava exhorts care with the Sages’ words through an exposition of Ecclesiastes.
Why were weighty rabbinic teachings not written in the Torah?
The verse says that making books has no end.
What does the verse’s weariness of flesh mean?
One exposition treats it as a warning against mocking the Sages.
Rava points out that the verse says meditation, not mockery.
He reads meditation on their words as nourishing pleasure.
A baraita relates how a prison guard spilled half of the water brought to Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Akiva tells his attendant that his survival depends on the water supplied.
He asks to wash his hands despite the attendant’s concern that too little remains to drink.
He chooses observance of the Sages’ handwashing rule despite the danger.
He eats only after washing, prompting the Sages to praise his lifelong care.
A heavenly voice praises Solomon’s enactments of courtyard eiruv and handwashing.
Rava introduces an exposition of the Song of Songs invitation to fields and vineyards.
Israel asks to be judged by Torah scholars studying in hardship rather than urban sins.
The villages are reread as those who denied God despite receiving good.
Vineyards become study houses; vine, blossoms, and pomegranates become Bible, Mishna, and Gemara learners.
Rav Hamnuna describes Solomon’s many parables and reasons for Torah and scribal words.
Rava reads Ecclesiastes as Solomon teaching through accent marks and comparisons.
Ulla compares Solomon’s explanations to handles added to a basket of Torah.
Mar Ukva derives many laws from even the small strokes of Torah letters.
The next exposition begins asking in whom Torah words are found.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier exposition praises those who study Torah early and late.
Rabba instead praises one who endures deprivation for Torah.
Rava invokes sacrifice for Torah study and tells of Rav Adda bar Mattana’s exchange with his wife.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets the verse about God repaying those who hate Him.
Rabbi Ila contrasts prompt punishment with delayed reward for the righteous.
Doing commandments today and receiving reward tomorrow are derived from the verse.
Why does the divine description use a plural form for patience?
The patience extends both to the righteous and to the wicked.
Does Rabbi Yehuda’s two-beit-seah cap include the well and the area between posts or only the well?
The alternatives turn on whether a person notices the well or the surrounding enclosure and might confuse it with a karpef.
A baraita states Rabbi Yehuda’s cap and the Rabbis’ comparison with much larger fully walled spaces.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar allows a two-by-two-beit-seah well with only cow-length space to the posts.
His focus on the well seems to imply Rabbi Yehuda counted both well and post area.
Rabbi Yehuda too may have counted the well alone.
If so, how do the two views differ?
They differ on a long narrow enclosure.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes dwellings used internally from shelters serving open land.
The mishna disputes whether a public path through well posts must be diverted.
Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar describe the Rabbis’ rule as demonstrating the strength of partitions.
Rabbi Yohanan’s ruling on Jerusalem’s unlocked gates suggests he does not accept that rule.
He may have described the Rabbis’ view without agreeing.
The authorities’ positions appear to contradict their positions in another case.
A Tosefta lets Rabbi Yehuda use posts or beams between two houses but records the Rabbis’ refusal.
How can each view be reconciled across the two cases?
Rabbi Yehuda relies on two full house walls, unlike the well-post arrangement.
The Rabbis allow the well case because it has a nominal partition on all four sides.
Rabbi Yohanan is reported as exempting carrying in the Land of Israel from public-domain liability.
Abaye asks Rav Dimi for the basis of that reported ruling.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Natural borders cannot explain the ruling, since rivers surround Babylonia and the ocean surrounds the world.
Rav Dimi recognizes that Abaye has identified the real issue.
A second report limits Rabbi Yohanan’s ruling to steep ascents and descents unlike the desert camp.
Does public traffic turn a steep ten-handbreadth mound into public domain?
The Rabbis would preserve its private status because even easier well-post traffic does not undo a partition.
Would Rabbi Yehuda distinguish this difficult passage from easy well-post traffic?
Rava still treats it as public domain, even for a rope-assisted climb or Beit Meron.
A traversed courtyard is private for Shabbat but public for doubtful impurity.
If the Rabbis already accept well posts, the courtyard seems too obvious; perhaps Rabbi Yehuda taught it.
The novelty under the Rabbis is its public status for impurity.
A mishna likewise separates the Shabbat and impurity status of paths opening by pits or caves.
The path wording is corrected from in the pits to toward the pits.
Its difficult passage again appears too obvious for the Rabbis and thus evidence about Rabbi Yehuda.
Its public status for impurity remains the new point under the Rabbis.
Beit Gilgul paths are also private for Shabbat and public for impurity.
The school of Rabbi Yannai defines these paths by inability to run while carrying a seah.
Again, the Shabbat rule appears obvious for the Rabbis and seems to reflect Rabbi Yehuda.
Joshua assigned easy roads to the public and difficult routes to individuals, explaining the private status.
The mishna permits posts for public cisterns, public wells, and private wells but requires a full wall for private cisterns, per Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava permits posts only at public wells and requires a ten-handbreadth rope belt elsewhere.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel rules for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava and limits well posts to living spring water.
Why state both restrictions?
The first ruling alone might still allow a public cistern of collected water.
The spring-water rule alone might still allow a private spring well.
The mishna permits carrying in a small walled garden or karpef with a dwelling feature or town adjacency.
Rabbi Yehuda also accepts a cistern, ditch, or cave within the enclosure.
Rabbi Akiva dispenses with those features within the stated square dimensions.
Rabbi Eliezer restricts a longer shape; Rabbi Yosei permits up to twice the breadth.
Rabbi Elai reports a larger karpef allowance from Rabbi Eliezer.
He reports a rule about the courtyard resident who omitted an eiruv.
He reports arkablin as Passover bitter herbs and says no other student confirmed the three rulings.
Why say furthermore for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava but not for Rabbi Yehuda’s consecutive strict rulings?
The Rabbis interrupted Rabbi Yehuda’s statements but not Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava’s.
Another mishna says furthermore despite the Rabbis interrupting Rabbi Eliezer.
There the interruption stayed on the same subject; here it changed subject.
The Gemara turns to Rabbi Akiva’s allowance without a dwelling feature.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: How does Rabbi Akiva differ from the first tanna’s size limit?
A very small amount separates their measurements.
A baraita says the Sages did not specify that tiny excess beyond seventy cubits and a remainder.
Two beit seah equal the Tabernacle courtyard’s area.
What is the source for converting that area to a square?
The courtyard verse is read as redistributing fifty cubits to square its area.
What does the verse mean in its plain description?
Abaye places the Tabernacle within the courtyard with clear space before and beside it.
A baraita lets Rabbi Eliezer accept length up to twice breadth, unlike the apparent mishna wording.
Rav Beivai reads the mishna’s limit as more than twice the breadth too.
How then does Rabbi Eliezer differ from Rabbi Yosei?
The dispute turns on a squared or diagonal measure.
Two reports of Shmuel rule leniently for Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Akiva’s ruling removes any requirement for a booth or dwelling.
Rabbi Yosei’s ruling permits the long and narrow shape.
A residential karpef over two beit seah loses its status if mostly sown, but not if mostly planted with trees.
Rav Huna limits the sown-area prohibition to more than two beit seah.
Rabbi Shimon treats roofs, yards, and karpefs as one domain for objects resting there at Shabbat’s onset.
Even Rabbi Shimon’s view may be challenged when most of the karpef is sown.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A smaller planted part is absorbed into the majority, making the entire karpef count as sown.
In the stricter version, even a minority sown area of two beit seah forbids carrying under the Rabbis.
Rav Yirmeya transmits a lenient version: only a sown area greater than two beit seah forbids carrying, following Rabbi Shimon.
Avimi treats planted trees as residential only when arranged in rows.
Rav Nahman allows carrying even without rows.
Rav Huna explains an observed case of unordered trees by following Rav Nahman.
A nonresidential karpef can be re-enclosed by breaching more than ten cubits and rebuilding the wall.
Does breaching and rebuilding one cubit at a time produce the same result?
A mishna uses a pomegranate-sized opening as the measure for breaking a wooden vessel.
Do repeated repaired olive-sized holes combine into that measure?
Rabbi Yohanan recalls the rule for a sandal whose straps break and are repaired in sequence.
Why does the second break change its status when a repaired first strap is present?
The repaired object is considered a new entity; the same reasoning can combine sequential repairs.
Hizkiya praises Rabbi Yohanan’s insight into his own teaching.
Rav Kahana limits carrying in a large storage yard behind houses to four cubits.
Rav Nahman permits it if an entrance from a house preceded the enclosure, but not if opened later.
Why state the obvious case of opening before enclosure?
A threshing floor could make the enclosure seem intended for storage; the entrance still suffices.
The Sages first liken floodwater in a residential karpef to seed crops that cancel its residential use.
Rava’s ruling instead treats useful water like planted trees, preserving permission.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ameimar confines the water allowance to water fit for use.
Rav Ashi adds a proposed depth-and-area limit to the usable water.
The Gemara rejects that limit by comparison with a large fruit pile.
A large yard at Pum Nahara connects to a town and a vineyard path ending at a river bank.
How can carrying in this yard be permitted?
An added wall at the river bank would sit on an existing partition.
Camels would knock down a doorway frame at the vineyard path.
Abaye proposes a side post at the path entrance that would also serve the yard.
Rava fears people would infer side posts work on ordinary open vineyard paths.
He proposes a side post at the town entrance that also serves the yard.
Carrying within the town and within the yard is thereby permitted.
Rav Aha and Ravina disagree on carrying between the town and yard.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior dispute concerns whether the empty yard’s lack of residents permits transfer from the town.
Planting trees does not reduce a nonresidential karpef’s measured area.
A ten-high, four-wide pillar reduces it; Rabba and Rava dispute a pillar between three and four wide.
Rabba counts the narrower pillar because it is outside the lavud range.
Rava requires a significant place four handbreadths wide.
A new residential wall works four handbreadths from the old wall but is disputed at three to four.
Rabba counts it as separate once beyond lavud.
Rava still requires four handbreadths of separation.
In Rav Simi’s lenient version, firm plaster reduces the area; weak attached plaster is disputed.
Rabba counts plaster that presently stands.
Rava excludes plaster unable to stand by itself.
A wall four handbreadths from a mound works; nearer or on its edge is disputed.
Rav Hisda’s other ruling identifies him as accepting a wall atop a wall for Shabbat.
Even the opposing view accepts the upper wall for carrying on the mound itself.
What if the lower wall sinks while the upper wall remains?
Is this a question about acquiring a convert’s ownerless property?
The turnip-seed case shows later improvement cannot retroactively establish possession.
The issue concerns Shabbat, where a partition arising that day is legally recognized.
Rav Nahman seemingly recognizes such a wall only for liability, not permitted carrying.
That restriction applies to a deliberately erected Shabbat wall.
A woman’s wall atop a wall fails to acquire ownerless land; a man’s plowing succeeds.
Rava and Rabbi Zeira dispute whether roofing one of three beit seah reduces the open karpef.
Does this parallel Rav and Shmuel’s dispute over an open veranda?
Rav imagines a descending roof edge as a wall; Shmuel does not.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A flat veranda roof would be agreed; the karpef case has a slanted roof edge.
Rabbi Zeira agrees that a karpef fully breached into a courtyard exceeds its permitted size.
Rav Yosef asks how a previously permitted courtyard can make the karpef forbidden.
Abaye points to the newly opened space once occupied by the fallen wall.
Rav Hisda permits the courtyard while forbidding the breached karpef.
Would remnants of wall not sometimes favor the karpef instead?
The fallen-wall area pushes the size-limited karpef over its limit; the residential courtyard has no such limit.
An orchard loses the outer mansion wall it relied on, and Rav Beivai proposes an inner wall.
Rav Pappi rejects that inner wall because it was constructed for the house, not the orchard.
The Exilarch seeks a way to carry through his large orchard to a pavilion on Shabbat.
Rav Huna erects closely spaced reed partitions; Rava begins a response continued on the next daf.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava removes Rav Huna’s reeds, and two students gather them to prevent their replacement.
Ravina compares the orchard to a new town walled before settlement, whose limit begins at habitation.
Rav Pappa cites architects’ privacy screens as walls that do not count for residence.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua cites a wall serving objects rather than dwelling.
The separate eiruvs of Mehoza’s rows illustrate the weakness of cattle-ditch partitions.
The Exilarch reproaches the scholars for undoing a useful arrangement before Shabbat.
Rabbi Elai’s large-karpef allowance is contrasted with Hananya’s still larger allowance.
Rabbi Yohanan traces both measures to the city/courtyard reading of Isaiah’s verse.
The authorities differ over the size of an intermediate town.
Why was Isaiah in Hezekiah’s courtyard?
He established a Torah gathering near the sick king.
The account suggests gathering study at an ill scholar’s entrance.
The Gemara cautions that this could provoke an accuser against the patient.
The discussion returns to Rabbi Elai’s rule for a resident who forgot the eiruv.
Another mishna forbids carrying to and from the house for both that resident and the others.
Rav Sheshet begins reconciling the texts as differing tannaitic views.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One text follows Rabbi Eliezer, the other the Rabbis.
They differ over whether ceding courtyard rights also cedes rights to the house.
Why is this explanation needed if the dispute seems obvious?
The added point concerns five courtyard residents, one of whom omitted the eiruv.
Rabbi Eliezer allows ceding to one resident; the Rabbis require ceding to each.
A five-person baraita requiring only one cession is assigned to Rabbi Eliezer.
Another transmission attributes that application directly to Rav Sheshet.
What if a person expressly states the opposite of each side’s presumed house-rights transfer?
One possibility makes Rabbi Eliezer’s house transfer only a presumption that express words can override.
The other makes house and courtyard inseparable, leaving the contrary statement ineffective.
For the Rabbis, an express house transfer might override their usual presumption.
Or their rule might make surrendering both house and courtyard impossible.
Abaye holds that explicit intent controls under either opinion.
Reish Lakish identifies the arkablin herb named in Rabbi Elai’s Passover report.
The chapter on well posts concludes.
The new mishna allows eiruv, shared alley food, and second-tithe purchases with most foods, excluding water and salt.
Wine can serve a nazirite’s eiruv and teruma an Israelite’s, while Sumakhos requires ordinary food.
A priest’s eiruv may be placed in a plowed grave field; Rabbi Yehuda extends the placement to graves.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The priest can reach the eiruv among graves while avoiding contact with impurity.
Rabbi Yohanan warns that general rules can have unlisted exceptions even when they say except.
Which rule prompted that warning if it was not the present mishna?
A mishna divides positive commandments by whether they depend on time.
Matza, festival joy, and assembly oblige women despite being time-bound.
Torah study, procreation, and firstborn redemption exempt them despite not being time-bound.
These exceptions establish that a general rule need not be exhaustive.
Another mishna gives a broad impurity rule for what carries a zav or carries him.
Does it omit an object used for riding?
The saddle’s upper grip is a riding accessory distinct from a seat.
This again limits reliance on an apparently exhaustive general statement.
Truffles and mushrooms are omitted exceptions to the eiruv rule naming only water and salt.
Two amoraim attach the mixed water-and-salt rule to either eiruv or second-tithe purchases.
On the eiruv reading, mixing water and salt makes them usable together.
On the second-tithe reading, the mixture can be bought with second-tithe money.
The second-tithe allowance implies eiruv allowance, but not conversely, because tithe requires produce.
Rabbi Yitzhak transmits the second-tithe version.
A fish-brine report is challenged as perhaps involving fish innards mixed into the brine.
The brine case contains fish substance and does not establish that water and salt alone may be bought.
Rav Yosef begins a further qualification on the next daf.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yosef requires oil added to the water-and-salt mixture.
Abaye asks why the oil alone would not establish permission.
The water and salt are paid for within an increased oil price.
Can an otherwise ineligible item be bought by bundling its price?
Ben Bag Bag derives bundled hide, fleece, jug, and fermented drink from the tithe verse.
Rabbi Yohanan asks why the verse specifically includes oxen if the other items suffice.
Oxen alone might allow attached hide but not a sheep’s fleece.
Sheep alone might allow attached fleece but not wine together with its jug.
Wine alone might allow its needed jug but not fermented mead.
Starting from strong drink could mean fruit, leaving wine’s jug uncertain.
Adding wine still leaves fleece uncertain, so the sheep clause is needed.
Why then is the oxen clause needed once sheep and fleece are included?
Trying to assign oxen to hide only leaves the sheep wording available to include fleece, so oxen remains redundant.
Rabbi Yohanan’s challenge is thus repeated.
What interpretive method divides the fish-brine authorities from the following tanna’im?
One side uses amplification and restriction; the other uses general and particular terms.
Amplification, restriction, and renewed amplification include most things while excluding brine or water and salt.
The alternate general-particular-general reading includes what resembles the listed products.
Another baraita describes the relevant resemblance as offspring of the earth’s offspring.
What practical difference separates these two definitions?
Abaye identifies fish: one definition includes them as earth-grown, the other traces them to water.
The Gemara begins challenging Abaye’s classification of fish as earth-grown.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The different lash counts for water insects and land insects undermine classifying fish as earth-grown.
Ravina instead distinguishes the two tithe readings through birds, which some count as earth-grown.
Why does one reading include birds and the other exclude them?
One gives weight to the final general term and includes things similar in two respects.
The other gives weight to the first general term and requires resemblance in three respects.
Rav allows eiruvs with several modest herbs but excludes green grain and unripe dates.
A baraita warns that sweet clover may be harmful and its hardened seed inedible.
Rav may mean soft clover eaten by people with many children.
Alternatively, food edible to others can support an eiruv, like wine for a nazirite.
Or he means a superior Median clover.
Another ruling of Rav allows green grain and assigns it the ground-fruit blessing.
Rav revised his view after observing that people in Babylonia eat it.
A baraita says unusual planting choices do not determine general food status.
The answer begins distinguishing a commonly eaten garden variety on the next daf.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav refers to green grain of a garden variety.
How are arugula seeds edible?
Earlier generations crushed them as a condiment for roasted meat.
Rabbi Zeira rests at the study-house entrance and honors scholars passing by.
A child reports separate blessings for dodder and green grain.
Rabbi Zeira reasons that the plant drawing from earth should receive the ground-fruit blessing.
The child’s ruling prevails: ripeness governs the blessing, and dodder also draws sustenance from earth.
A baraita treats unripe dates as food for tithe purchase and impurity, apparently against Rav.
Rabbi Yehuda likewise calls them fruit while exempting them from tithes.
The first proposal assigns the baraita to palms whose fruit never ripens.
Rabbi Yehuda elsewhere requires tithes for such dates, contradicting that proposal.
Food-impurity status differs from eiruv suitability; cooking could make the fruit edible.
Where was Rabbi Yohanan’s cooking principle stated?
A baraita debates tithing almonds at different stages and records a lenient ruling.
How could large bitter almonds be suitable if the stricter opinion tithes them?
Cooking can sweeten them and make them edible.
How does Rabbi Yehuda’s heart-of-palm ruling differ from the first tanna’s?
Abaye proposes a difference after boiling or frying it.
A baraita shows that boiling can make otherwise inedible animal parts susceptible to food impurity.
Rava instead locates the difference in the blessing before eating heart of palm.
Rav Yehuda calls it ground fruit; Shmuel uses the general blessing because it hardens.
Shmuel acknowledges the radish analogy: it hardens yet takes a ground-fruit blessing.
Radishes are grown for soft eating, unlike palms grown for their hearts; Shmuel’s blessing prevails.
The discussion returns to Rav’s eiruv rule and a handful measure for dodder.
Green grain requires a full farmers’ bundle.
Edible greens used to make glasswort require a handful.
Rabbi Yannai permits moist beans for an eiruv in a handful measure.
Rav Hamnuna permits raw beets for an eiruv.
Rav Hisda’s warning about raw beets challenges their suitability.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior warning concerns partly cooked beets.
An alternate report bars raw beets from an eiruv because of Rav Hisda’s health warning.
People eat them without dying.
The danger concerns partial cooking.
Rav Hisda praises thoroughly cooked beets, and Abaye describes the needed boil.
Rava offers to answer questions and is asked the apple measure for an eiruv.
Rava initially doubts that apples can serve as an eiruv.
A mishna says foods combine toward the two-meal eiruv measure and food-impurity measure.
Does its word all prove apples are included despite unlisted exceptions to general rules?
The linked impurity measure supports their inclusion as food.
What quantity of apples is needed?
Rav Nahman requires a kav.
A baraita’s five-peach gift and its reported eiruv parallel seem to suggest a smaller fruit measure.
Peaches have greater significance than apples.
Rav Yosef says his teaching was misattributed to the baraita rather than a mishna.
The mishna lists minimum poor-tithe portions of staples, fruit, wine, oil, and other foods.
Why prefer the mishna when each source includes items not eaten alone?
Its half-log of wine matches Rav’s eiruv amount of two quarter-logs.
Rav Yosef first thinks each of the two meals needs its own full food portion.
Rabba allows mixed fractions of the meals to combine.
Why require two quarter-logs of wine when a baraita seems to require less?
The baraita speaks of concentrated cooked wine.
Two versions specify vinegar enough to dip food for two meals.
The baraita measures olives and onions as accompaniments to two meals.
Rabbi Meir once rejected an onion eiruv and confined its maker to four cubits.
The rejection concerns onion leaves, while the edible bulbs are permitted.
A further qualification about onion leaves begins on the next daf.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The harmful onion leaves are those on bulbs smaller than a span.
Rav Pappa adds that drinking beer afterward removes the concern.
A baraita warns about onion toxins and tells of Rabbi Hanina’s recovery.
Shmuel allows beer for an eiruv and treats three log of it as invalidating a ritual bath.
Why is the bath rule not obvious from dye-water?
Dye-water retains the name water, while beer has a different name.
How much beer supports an eiruv? A proposal requires two quarter-logs.
The proposal compares wine and other liquids in the carrying-measure mishna.
Carrying requires a significant amount; an eiruv can use the beer customarily drunk at two meals.
How many dates are needed for an eiruv?
Rav Yosef requires a kav.
He cites a baraita praising repayment of eaten dried figs with dates.
Why praise a payment equal in monetary value?
Rav Yosef proposes equal volume, making the dates substantially more valuable.
Abaye instead explains that equally priced dates are easier for the priest to sell.
Measures are given for roasted-flour food and roasted grain used in an eiruv.
Abaye reports that roasted grain benefits the heart and eases anxious thoughts.
Abaye reports a folk remedy for weakness of the heart.
Shmuel distinguishes eiruv amounts for a relish, a stand-alone food, and raw meat.
Rabba and Rav Yosef differ over whether roasted meat is relish or stand-alone food.
Rav Yosef cites Persian practice of eating roast meat without bread.
Abaye questions making one region’s custom the general rule.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review
